items.claim: The R5 supersession-retirement path checks only that a supersession record carries the four required KEYS (supersedes_cure_id, recorded, ordered_by, why); it does not verify that old_artifact_sha256 matches the claim it purports to retire, nor that ordered_by names a ruling that actually exists. A well-formed but factually false supersession record therefore retires any named cure_id to SUPERSEDED - a non-ACCEPTED, non-blocking status - without any check on the record's truthfulness.
items.suggested_fix: Require old_artifact_sha256 in a supersession record to match the artifact_sha256 actually recorded on the claim it supersedes (cross-check against the claims already parsed from the same file), and/or require ordered_by to name a ruling id that a caller can optionally cross-verify against the controlling-rulings file. Low priority: this does not let anything read ACCEPTED, and R5's own authorization model (a controlling-agent ruling) is presumably enforced upstream of this tool, not by it - but the gap is worth disclosing since OW-10 exists specifically to prevent unverified self-reported closure.
items.orchestrator_proposed_disposition: PROPOSED (the controlling agent rules): adopt the suggested fix. A supersession record must carry old_artifact_sha256 equal to the artifact_sha256 of the claim it retires, cross-checked against the claims parsed from the same file, and an ordered_by naming an execution id of the form <attempt_id>#e<N>. A record failing either check is REFUSED, not honoured. The reviewer's adversarial fixture becomes a selftest refusal vector. No cure is re-opened: nothing read ACCEPTED through the gap, and the one genuine supersession record (EZEK-P0-CURE-toolkit, old_artifact_sha256 06b0e7a6..., ordered_by ezek_controlling_rulings_a1#e2 ruling R5) is expected to pass the tightened check, which is to be proven before it is relied on. The changed verifier goes to the distinct checker who spot-reviews the author wave, bound to its new digest.
